planting.note: Sow fresh seed directly on the soil surface in fall and let winter cold and moisture break dormancy; seed needs a cold-moist period before it will germinate the following spring.

directions: Tuck this diminutive, cold-loving violet into cool, humus-rich, often slightly rocky or calcareous woodland soil where summer heat stays moderated by deep shade, since it struggles in warm lowland gardens south of its northern range. The pale lilac flowers carry a distinctively long, straight spur behind the petals and appear just as the heart-shaped leaves unfurl in early-to-mid spring. Keep the planting site consistently moist but never waterlogged, mimicking the mossy rock outcrops and cool ravine slopes where it grows naturally across the northern forests of North America, Europe, and Asia. Division of established clumps in early spring is more reliable than seed for increasing a planting.

planting.note: Sow seed directly on moist, humus-rich soil in fall so it overwinters outdoors and experiences the cold-moist stratification needed to trigger spring germination.

directions: Plant this small boreal violet in cool, consistently moist, acidic soil beneath conifers or mixed northern hardwoods, where its rounded, kidney-shaped leaves with a distinctive notched base form low, slowly spreading tufts. Small white flowers with fine purple veining on the lower petal appear in spring, followed by self-fertile cleistogamous flowers later in the season that set most of the seed. Mulch with leaf litter or pine duff to hold moisture and keep roots cool through summer, since this species is poorly suited to hot, humid, or dry conditions. It is best suited to northern gardens and cool microclimates rather than warm-summer regions.

planting.note: Scatter seed on moist prepared soil in fall or press into place in early spring; cold-moist stratification over winter improves germination the following season.

directions: Site this stemless eastern violet in moist, humus-rich soil at the edge of woods, floodplain terraces, or damp meadows, where it tolerates more sun than many of its deep-woods relatives as long as moisture stays reliable. Deep violet-blue flowers with a pale, bearded throat rise above dark green, long-petioled leaves in mid-spring, and the plant spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a loose patch. It is easily confused with the more common Viola sororia, but its leaves are typically narrower and more pointed and the flowering stems hold the blossoms slightly above the foliage. Keep soil from drying out during the growing season, especially in its first year of establishment.

planting.note: Sow directly on moist soil in fall so winter cold stratifies the seed; established clumps can also be divided in early spring.

directions: Grow this leafy-stemmed violet in moist, humus-rich soil along stream banks, open woods, and shaded roadside seeps, where it forms loose mats from slender rhizomes. Unlike the stemless violets, its pale blue-violet flowers are carried on leafy aerial stems alongside the heart-shaped leaves, and the flower's spur is short, thick, and rounded rather than slender. It tolerates slightly more light than deep-shade violets but still needs consistent moisture and appreciates a position with morning sun and afternoon shade. Let it self-seed and spread naturally at a woodland edge or rain garden margin, where it makes an unobtrusive, long-lived native groundcover.

common_name: Confederate Violet (Pale Blue Form of Common Violet)

planting.note: Sow seed or set divisions on moist, prepared soil in fall or early spring; this naturally occurring color form of the common blue violet self-seeds and spreads readily once established.

directions: This long-cultivated color form of the common blue violet was first collected in Tennessee and named for the pale, frosty-white petals washed with a central thumbprint of blue-violet veining that gives it a distinctive icy appearance in the lawn or shade border. Plant it in ordinary moist garden soil under high shade from deciduous trees, where it blooms heavily in early spring and again sporadically into early summer. Like the species, it self-seeds and spreads by short rhizomes, so give it room to naturalize in an informal woodland-edge planting, lawn, or groundcover bed rather than a tightly controlled perennial border. Deadheading spent flowers is unnecessary, since the plant also produces hidden self-pollinating flowers at ground level later in the season that quietly replenish the colony.

planting.note: Set divisions or sow seed on moist prepared soil in fall or early spring; this selection comes true enough from its own seed to naturalize a patch of speckled flowers over a few seasons.

directions: Choose this selection of the common blue violet for its white flowers finely stippled with violet-blue speckles across all five petals, a more uniformly freckled pattern than the bold central blaze of Confederate violet. Plant in moist, humus-rich soil beneath deciduous shade, where the low rosettes of heart-shaped leaves and short flowering stems make an easy-care groundcover for a woodland path edge or shaded lawn. It spreads readily by self-sown seed and short rhizomes, so site it where naturalizing is welcome rather than in a tightly maintained bed. Established plantings need little care beyond occasional division to keep them within bounds and consistent moisture during dry spells.
